uncertainty: Whether a Mexican owner-operator will let an outside firm contact *his customers* about overdue invoices. That is the single hinge on the pivot I'm recommending — collections is relationship-sensitive in a way reporting is not, and no amount of product work resolves it. You find out by asking five owners for permission to chase five invoices next week, not by building.
headline: Right pain, wrong product. You've built a reporting service, priced it like software, and you already wrote down the reason it won't retain — the disappearance test answers itself.
category: SMB cash operations / outsourced finance function for Mexican formal SMBs (8–25 employees) — currently expressed as a weekly reporting SaaS-plus-human service
buyer: The **dueño-operador** of a formal 8–25 employee company in GDL/CDMX/MTY — usually the founder, sometimes with an administrative assistant who handles invoicing. He signs, but he does not decide alone: the **contador externo** is the de facto gatekeeper on anything touching CFDI, bank credentials or SAT access. Your research is unambiguous that the accountant is simultaneously your only credible distribution channel and your most motivated competitor. Treat the accountant as a second buyer with veto power, not as a bystander.
priceBand:
Three anchors are already set in this buyer's head, and yours sits in the worst part of the gap:

- **Cloud accounting software:** MXN 229–499/month (Alegra, TuKonta). This is what "software that shows me my cash" costs in Mexico.
- **The despacho contable:** roughly MXN 1,500–4,000/month for a 10-person firm, and it includes full fiscal compliance — the thing the owner believes he legally must buy.
- **Fractional/virtual CFO despacho:** MXN 8,000–25,000/month, sold as human judgement.

Your MXN 2,500–7,000 lands **on top of the accountant's fee for a deliverable the owner thinks he's already paying for**, and at 5–20× the software anchor. The band is not indefensible — MXN 4,000–6,000 is very defensible for *executed work* — but it is nearly impossible to defend for *a report*. Price the service, and make the service something the owner cannot do on Sunday night with a spreadsheet.
theIdea: A digital cash-management and financial-operations system for Mexican SMBs of roughly 8–25 employees in Guadalajara, Mexico City and Monterrey — companies with meaningful cash volume, no internal finance person, and an external accountant who handles invoicing and SAT compliance but does not tell the owner whether he'll make payroll in six weeks.
theSolution: The customer connects or uploads bank statements, CFDI invoices, AP/AR, payroll obligations, recurring expenses and cash movements. The platform categorises everything and produces a weekly cash summary, a 30/60/90-day forecast, a list of overdue customer payments, upcoming supplier and tax obligations, missing-document alerts, and three recommended actions. Phase 1 is assisted: a trained financial operator reviews the AI output before it reaches the client. Phase 2 automates categorisation, matching, forecasting and reporting as the system learns patterns. Monetisation is a monthly subscription of MXN 2,500–7,000.
valueProposition:
"You already pay an accountant and you still don't know your cash position. Every Monday you'll know what you have, what's coming in, what's going out, and the three things to do about it."

That is a clean and true proposition. It is also, per your own research, **a sentence a vendor blog has already written** — the pain is recognised and being marketed against by Alegra, CONTPAQi, Bind and every despacho upselling *asesoría financiera*. The proposition is correct and unowned. Being correct is not the same as being defensible.
whyThisCouldWork:
Let me give you the genuine tailwinds before I take the product apart, because they're real and they're why this is a flip and not a kill.

**1. The pain is structurally created, not invented.** The Mexican SMB finance stack is optimised for SAT compliance, not for decisions. The accountant's job is to keep you out of trouble with the tax authority; nobody is paid to tell the owner he runs out of cash on the 14th. A company with 8–25 employees is too big for the shoebox and too small to hire a controller at MXN 35–60k/month. That is a real structural hole and it does not close on its own.

**2. QuickBooks exiting Mexico in April 2023 created genuine displacement.** Thousands of owners who wanted an easy cloud service got orphaned. Alegra has been absorbing them, but displacement means switching behaviour is currently unusually available in this market. That window narrows every quarter.

**3. Ingestion is cheap now, which means you can start small.** Belvo aggregates 60+ institutions across MX/BR/CO and ships an explicit "Fiscal Mexico" SAT product; Finerio Connect and Prometeo are alternatives. Ten years ago this idea required two years of bank integration work. Today it's an API key. **This is a tailwind for your cost of entry and a headwind for your moat — the same fact does both.**

**4. Forward-looking cash forecasting for sub-25-employee firms is genuinely thin.** Your research found it: the category is mature on compliance, semi-mature on cloud bookkeeping, and actually underserved on 30/60/90 forecasting for this size band. That is real whitespace. But note the precise finding — *it's a feature, not a category.* Whitespace that can be filled by a sprint at Alegra is a head start, not a moat.

**5. Your unit economics are survivable if you're disciplined.** At MXN 4,000 ARPU, one financial operator at MXN 30k loaded handling ~20 clients gives you ~37% COGS on delivery. That's a services business, not a software business, but it's a real business — provided churn is low. Churn is exactly the problem.

**6. And credit where it's due: your self-awareness is unusually high.** The answers to "Why Hard To Copy," "Moat That Isn't" and "Disappearance Test" are more honest than 90% of what founders write. You have already diagnosed this correctly in prose. Your numbers just haven't caught up with your prose.
biggestRisk:
**You will win pilots and lose renewals, because information does not create dependency.**

Read your own disappearance test again: *"If we disappeared tomorrow the owner would go back to asking their accountant and guessing from the bank balance. That is what they do today. It would hurt but it would not stop the business."* Then read your lock-in score: 8/10.

Those two statements cannot both be true. A product whose absence "would hurt but would not stop the business" is a 3, maybe a 4. And the specific failure mode is worse than generic churn, because your product's value **decays as it succeeds**. Month one, the owner learns something genuinely alarming — his DSO is 68 days, three clients owe him MXN 400k, he's paying two subscriptions he forgot about. Month two, he acts on it. Month three, he has now internalised the shape of his own business, has asked his assistant to build a tab in Excel, and the Monday email tells him things he already knows. He cancels in month five and does not feel any loss. This is the classic dashboard death spiral, and it kills at MXN 2,500 just as reliably as at MXN 7,000 — arguably faster at MXN 2,500, because low price signals low consequence.

**The "accumulated historical data" moat is not a moat here, and I want to be precise about why.** Your data's source of truth is the bank and the SAT. Both are re-ingestible by any competitor in an afternoon, retroactively, for years back — CFDI history is downloadable from the SAT, bank history comes through Belvo. You are not accumulating proprietary data; you are caching public-to-the-client data that anyone with the client's consent can re-pull. Compare a genuine data moat: a payments processor's default-risk history, or a payroll provider's per-employee record that exists nowhere else. Yours is not that. The only genuinely proprietary asset you accumulate is the *categorisation and matching corrections your operators make* — and those are worth something to your model, not to your customer's switching cost.

Second-order: the MXN 2,500–7,000 price against a MXN 229–499 anchor means every renewal conversation is a re-justification. Services at 10× the software price survive only when the buyer can name a peso outcome. "I know my cash position" is not a peso outcome. "You recovered MXN 180,000 I'd written off" is.
secondRisk:
**The accountant is your channel and your assassin, and Alegra has already armed him.**

Every structural fact points the same direction. The despacho holds the CFDI access, the bank statements, the client relationship and the credibility. He is asked "should I buy this?" and he has three reasons to say no: it makes his own reporting look thin, it introduces a third party into a relationship he monetises, and — critically — **he can sell it himself.** Your Phase 1 is a trained human reviewing AI output and sending a weekly summary. That is *exactly* what a virtual-CFO despacho already sells, at overlapping prices, with an existing client list and zero customer-acquisition cost.

And the tooling is being handed to him. Alegra explicitly builds for despachos with multi-RFC included so one accountant subscription manages every client company at no extra per-RFC cost. CONTPAQi Bancos already reads the major Mexican bank layouts, validates received CFDI against the SAT's Administrador de Documentos Digitales, and shows a traffic-light reconciliation dashboard. CONTPAQi is publishing AI/automation marketing. The incumbents are not asleep, and their route to your customer is shorter than yours.

Third risk worth naming even though you didn't ask: **adjacent fintechs hold better cards than you do.** Clara has the card transaction data and the finance-team relationship. Xepelin built receivables/payables plus a financial dashboard for Mexican SMBs off SAT data — that is close enough to your core that you should treat it as prior art until proven otherwise. Higo, Konfío, Mendel, Kapital and Fondeadora all sit within one feature of your product. They have the data, the balance sheet, and a reason to give a cash forecast away free because their revenue comes from credit and interchange. **You cannot win a feature fight against a company that can price your product at zero.** Verify what Xepelin and Higo already ship before you write another line of code.
validationPlan:
Four weeks, no engineering, roughly MXN 40–60k. Every step has a written pass/fail. Do them in this order.

**Week 1 — The number test (kills the vague version of this idea)**

Recruit 15 dueños-operadores of 8–25 employee firms across GDL and CDMX. Route: ask 3 despachos and 2 industry chambers (Coparmex, CANACINTRA local chapters) for WhatsApp introductions. Offer MXN 500 Amazon credit for 30 minutes.

In each call, do not describe your product. Ask exactly four things:
1. "How much did your customers owe you as of last Friday?" — Time how long it takes and whether the number arrives at all.
2. "Which single invoice is most overdue, and by how many days?"
3. "What's the largest amount you've written off in the last 12 months because you stopped chasing it?"
4. "Who chases overdue invoices today — you, your assistant, or nobody?"

**Pass:** ≥8 of 15 cannot answer Q1 within two minutes, AND ≥6 name a write-off of MXN 50,000+. **Fail:** most of them answer instantly from their ERP or their assistant's spreadsheet — in which case the pain is administrative, not financial, and your price band collapses.

**Week 2 — The concierge collections test (this is the real experiment)**

Take the 5 most painful cases from Week 1. Offer this, free, for 30 days: *"Give me your aged receivables list. My team will contact your overdue customers, follow up weekly, and report to you every Monday. You approve the tone and the list before we send anything."* Run it in Google Sheets and WhatsApp. No product.

Measure two things and write them down before you start:
- **Consent rate:** how many of 5 let you contact their customers at all. This is the make-or-break number for the entire pivot. If it's 1 or 2, the flip I'm recommending is wrong and you need Plan B below.
- **Pesos recovered in 30 days** and **days of DSO reduction.**

**Pass:** ≥3 of 5 grant consent, AND aggregate recovery ≥MXN 250,000 across the cohort. **Fail:** consent under 3, or recovery under MXN 100k — the human contact isn't what's blocking the money.

**Week 3 — The price test with real money**

Go back to the pilot cohort with a signed one-pager: MXN 5,900/month, 30-day cancellation, first month charged today via SPEI or Stripe. Do not offer a free tier and do not discount — a discount destroys the signal you're paying for. Simultaneously, present the same offer to 5 owners who did *not* get the free pilot, to separate reciprocity from willingness to pay.

**Pass:** 3+ paid conversions, at least 1 from the cold group. **Fail:** everyone loves it and nobody pays today. That is the answer to the question in your own "Biggest Risk" field.

**Week 4 — The channel test and the plumbing test, in parallel**

*Channel:* Pitch 10 despachos contables one thing: white-label. They bill their client MXN 4,000, you bill them MXN 1,200/RFC, their logo on the deliverable. Count three buckets: (a) yes, (b) no, (c) **"interesting — I'll build that myself."** If bucket (c) is 4 or more, direct sales is your only route and your CAC just doubled; plan accordingly.

*Plumbing:* Collect the actual bank list from your 15 interviewees. Open a Belvo and a Finerio sandbox and check each one. Expect coverage to be thinner than the marketing — one public tracker lists only 18 institutions reachable through Belvo, and coverage varies by product. Write down, per bank, whether you get live connection, file ingestion, or manual PDF. **If >40% of your prospects' banks require manual upload, your Phase 2 automation thesis is delayed by 18 months and your operator cost per client is structurally higher than modelled.** Better to know that in week 4 than in month 14.

**Plan B if the consent rate fails:** flip to the payables side instead — you run the payment calendar and the tax-obligation calendar, which is internal-facing and requires no third-party contact. Lower ceiling, but it still puts you inside the money workflow rather than beside it.
positioning:
You are currently positioned as **visibility** ("know your cash"). Visibility is a feature that Alegra sells for MXN 499 and that decays in value as the customer learns. Here are the two real alternatives, written as copy you could put on a landing page tomorrow.

---

**Option A — Visibility (your current position, sharpened)**

> ### Cada lunes a las 8:00 sabes exactamente cómo estás de dinero.
> Cuánto tienes. Cuánto te deben y quién. Cuánto debes esta semana y el mes que entra. Y las tres cosas que deberías hacer hoy.
>
> Tu contador te mantiene en orden con el SAT. Nosotros te decimos si vas a tener con qué pagar la nómina del 15.
>
> **Desde MXN 2,500 al mes. Sin instalar nada. Tu contador sigue siendo tu contador.**

*Why it fails commercially:* every claim here is an *information* claim. The buyer compares it to MXN 499 software and to the accountant he already pays. It sells beautifully in the first meeting and cancels in month five. It also invites the accountant to say "I can send you that."

---

**Option B — Execution (the flip)**

> ### Nosotros cobramos lo que te deben.
> Tú te dedicas a vender. Nosotros perseguimos cada factura vencida: seguimiento semanal a tus clientes, con el tono que tú apruebes, hasta que el dinero entra.
>
> Cada lunes recibes un reporte: cuánto entró, qué se cobró, qué sigue pendiente, y tus obligaciones de las próximas 4 semanas.
>
> **El mes pasado recuperamos MXN 1.4 millones que nuestros clientes ya habían dado por perdidos.**
>
> MXN 5,900 al mes. Si no recuperamos al menos tres veces eso en 90 días, no nos pagas el cuarto mes.

*Why it works:* the deliverable is **pesos in the bank**, not a chart. It self-justifies the price band without reference to the software anchor — nobody compares a collections service to Alegra. It creates real dependency: if you disappear, the chasing stops, and the owner knows within two weeks. It puts you inside the money workflow, which is where lock-in actually lives. And the guarantee converts your biggest risk ("will they pay MXN 2,500") into a sales asset.

---

**Recommendation: lead with B. Deliver A as the proof artifact.**

Sell collections and payables execution. Ship the weekly cash summary and the 30/60/90 forecast *inside* that service, as evidence of work performed. This changes almost nothing about what you build and almost everything about your defensibility:

- **Pricing power** rises because the value is denominated in recovered pesos, not in insight.
- **Lock-in** rises because removing you stops an operating process, not a report.
- **Copycat risk** drops meaningfully — Alegra and CONTPAQi are software companies; a labour-intensive, relationship-sensitive collections operation is genuinely off-strategy for them. Bind ERP's collections module sends *automated reminders*; that is not the same product and its existence actually validates the demand.
- **The accountant conflict softens.** "I'll do that myself" is a plausible response to a report. It is a much less plausible response to "I'll phone your client's client every Tuesday." Despachos do not want that work, which is precisely why it's yours.

One warning: the moment you *receive* funds rather than just chasing them, you inherit PLD/AML obligations and a much heavier regulatory load. Stay on the chasing side of that line — money moves bank-to-bank between your client and his customer, never through you.
finalAssessment:
**Flip. The insight is right; the wrapper is wrong; and you already knew it before I told you.**

What you got right: the buyer segment is real and structurally underserved. An 8–25 employee formal Mexican SMB has a compliance provider and no decision provider, and that gap doesn't self-close. Your prose diagnosis is unusually honest — *"the software is not hard to copy,"* *"I was thinking the AI is the moat but it probably isn't,"* and a disappearance test you wrote against your own interest. Most founders at this stage cannot do that.

What you got wrong is the gap between that prose and your scores. You rated lock-in 8/10 in the same assessment where you wrote that your absence "would not stop the business." You rated pricing power 7/10 while naming "will they pay 2,500 pesos a month" as your single biggest risk. Those aren't rounding errors; they're the two numbers your entire financial model depends on, and both are inflated by a factor of two. Three contradictions of 2+ points caps this at flip on the process alone — but the substance agrees with the process, which is the more important signal.

The research also removes two comfortable beliefs. First, ingestion is not a moat: Belvo sells bank aggregation plus a "Fiscal Mexico" SAT product off the shelf, so the integration work you named as defensible is a purchase order. Second, the assisted-service model is not novel: virtual-CFO despachos already sell your Phase 1 at overlapping prices with pre-existing client relationships. Your Phase 1 is not a bridge to a moat — it's a market you're entering late, against people who own the customer.

So here is the commercially honest version. **A weekly cash-visibility subscription at MXN 2,500–7,000 for Mexican SMBs will sell and will not retain.** You'll get 20–40 logos on charm and genuine pain, hold ~70% at month three, ~40% at month nine, and then discover your CAC never amortised because the LTV was 5 months. That path is not fatal, it's just expensive and slow to learn from.

The flip is to stop selling *knowledge of the cash problem* and start selling *the resolution of it*. Do the cobranza. Run the payables and tax calendar. Deliver the dashboard as evidence rather than as the product. Same technology, same segment, same price band — but the value becomes measurable in pesos, the churn logic inverts, and the software incumbents' path to copying you runs through a labour-intensive operation they have no appetite for.

**Three things to do this week, in order:** (1) Verify what Xepelin and Higo already ship for receivables and cash forecasting — if either already does concierge collections for this segment, everything above changes. (2) Run the Week-2 consent test with five owners; the consent rate is the highest-information number available to you at any price. (3) Stop calling it AI in the pitch. Your own answer says the AI is commodity, and in this buyer's ear "AI" reduces perceived accountability precisely when you need to charge for accountability.

What would move me from flip to build: consent rate of 4/5 or better in the collections test, aggregate 90-day recovery above 3× fees, and at least 3 despachos signing a white-label wholesale agreement rather than saying they'd build it. Get those three and you have a real business with a real moat — the moat just isn't the software, and it never was.

riskScores.label: Copycat Risk
riskScores.reasoning: Not a forecast — an observation. Alegra already pulls CFDI from the SAT, ingests bank statements, automates reconciliation and markets cash-flow statements plus AR/AP reporting, at MXN 499/month. CONTPAQi Bancos reads the major Mexican bank layouts, validates CFDI against the SAT's Administrador de Documentos Digitales, and ships a traffic-light reconciliation dashboard. misKuentas crosses statements against CFDI with difference detection. Bind ERP's collections module is explicitly positioned on improving cash flow. Belvo sells bank plus SAT ingestion as a product, so the integration work you named as defensible is a purchase order. And your Phase 1 assisted service is the existing business model of every virtual-CFO despacho in Guadalajara. The only thin whitespace is 30/60/90 forecasting for sub-25-employee firms — a feature, deliverable in one sprint by any of the above. 9 rather than 10 only because the *operational* discipline of a weekly human-reviewed delivery is genuinely unattractive to software incumbents.

riskScores.label: Platform Risk
riskScores.reasoning: Your 6 is close to fair, which is notable given the other three scores. Real fragility: Mexican bank connections have no mature open-banking mandate, aggregator coverage is thinner than marketed (one tracker lists just 18 institutions reachable via Belvo, with coverage varying by product), and a broken connection means the weekly deliverable fails — you correctly identified that trust erodes fast. Mitigations that keep this from an 8: three substitutable providers exist (Belvo, Finerio Connect, Prometeo); CFDI is fundamentally client-owned data retrievable from the SAT rather than a private platform's gift; the deliverable is weekly not real-time, so a human operator can patch a broken feed with a manual statement upload without the client noticing. That manual fallback is your insurance policy — but it is also a direct hit to Phase 2 margins, so price the labour in now.

riskScores.label: Lock-In Strength
riskScores.reasoning: The largest gap in the assessment, and your own disappearance test scores it for me: the owner "would go back to asking their accountant and guessing from the bank balance," which "would hurt but would not stop the business." That is a 3. The historical-records argument fails on inspection because your data's source of truth is the bank and the SAT — both re-ingestible retroactively by any competitor in an afternoon with the client's consent. You are caching, not accumulating. There is no proprietary record that dies with you, no configured workflow the client rebuilt his operations around, no third party who needs you in the loop. Worse, the value decays with success: once the owner has internalised his own cash shape, the Monday email starts telling him things he already knows. Lock-in only reaches 6+ if you move into the money workflow itself — chasing receivables, running the payment calendar — so that your removal stops a process rather than a report.

riskScores.label: Pricing Power
riskScores.reasoning: You are asking MXN 2,500–7,000 against a MXN 229–499 software anchor for visibly overlapping functionality, and sitting on top of a despacho fee of roughly MXN 1,500–4,000 that the client believes is mandatory. Meanwhile virtual-CFO despachos sell your exact Phase-1 model into pre-existing relationships. And your own biggest-risk answer is literally the willingness-to-pay question: "whether they will pay 2,500 pesos a month." A founder with 7/10 pricing power does not write that sentence. 4 rather than 2 because the deliverable does involve real human labour the buyer cannot self-supply, which supports *some* premium. It goes to 7 the moment the invoice can be justified in recovered pesos rather than in insight — which is the whole argument for the flip.

riskScores.label: Execution Risk
riskScores.reasoning: You are running a labour-intensive, quality-sensitive weekly service at MXN 2,500–7,000 ARPU across three cities simultaneously. Rough arithmetic: an operator at MXN 30k loaded handling ~20 clients puts delivery COGS near 37% at MXN 4,000 ARPU — workable, but zero tolerance for the mess you'll actually encounter. Real SMB inputs are photographed PDFs, WhatsApp voice notes, cash-in-a-drawer, invoices issued to the wrong RFC, and banks your aggregator doesn't cover. Every one of those becomes operator minutes, and a single bad forecast destroys the trust the whole subscription rests on. Then Phase 2 requires you to automate away exactly the human judgement your customers are paying for, without visible quality loss, before your margin gets squeezed. Layer on GDL+CDMX+MTY at once, plus a channel strategy that runs through people who may prefer to compete with you. Pick one city until the pilot cohort renews twice.

riskScores.label: Regulatory Risk
riskScores.reasoning: Moderate and manageable *as currently scoped*. You handle personal and financial data under the LFPDPPP, you'll almost certainly be asked to hold or use client SAT credentials (CIEC, and possibly e.firma) — a serious custody liability requiring real controls and explicit written mandate — and you'll be reading bank data via a licensed aggregator, which pushes most compliance onto them. You are not a regulated entity and you are not moving money. Two things change this: if you ever receive or disburse client funds you inherit PLD/AML obligations and a plausible need for licensing, taking this to 6–7; and if you make collections calls to your client's customers, you should verify PROFECO and CONDUSEF constraints on third-party collection practices before the first call. Keep money movement bank-to-bank between your client and his customer, never through your accounts.

contradictions.label: Lock-In Strength: rated 8/10, evidence supports 3/10
contradictions.quote: If we disappeared tomorrow the owner would go back to asking their accountant and guessing from the bank balance. That is what they do today. It would hurt but it would not stop the business.
contradictions.issue: This is a textbook description of weak lock-in, written by you, in the same assessment where you scored lock-in 8/10. "It would not stop the business" is the definition of a discretionary purchase. Your stated mechanism — holding historical records — doesn't rescue it: the bank and the SAT are the source of truth, and both are re-ingestible retroactively by any competitor the day after the client switches. You even hedged it yourself elsewhere: "The real moat if there is one is lock-in once we hold historical records." The "if there is one" is the honest part; the 8/10 is not. This matters commercially because your entire LTV assumption sits on this number — halve retention and your CAC never amortises.

contradictions.label: Pricing Power: rated 7/10, evidence supports 4/10
contradictions.quote: The real question is whether they will pay 2,500 pesos a month, connect their financial data, and actually use the recommendations every week.
contradictions.issue: You named willingness-to-pay at your floor price as your single biggest risk, then scored pricing power 7/10. Both cannot be true. The market data is against the 7: Alegra Contabilidad starts near MXN 499/month and entry plans run to MXN 229, for a product that already ships CFDI ingestion, bank reconciliation, cash-flow statements and AR/AP reporting. You are asking 5–20× that anchor while also sitting on top of an accountant's fee the owner already pays and considers non-negotiable. A 7/10 pricing power business does not need to ask whether the floor price clears.

contradictions.label: Copycat Risk: rated 7/10, evidence supports 9/10
contradictions.quote: Honestly, the software is not hard to copy. What would be hard is the accumulated per-customer financial history, the trust required to hand over financial data, and the relationships with accountants who could either block us or refer us.
contradictions.issue: Two of your three named barriers don't hold. The accumulated history is re-pullable from the SAT and the bank by anyone with client consent, so it's a cache and not an asset. Accountant relationships cut against you as often as for you — Alegra explicitly courts despachos with multi-RFC included at no extra cost per RFC, which arms your gatekeeper. Only the trust barrier is real, and trust is a race, not a wall. Meanwhile 9/10 isn't a prediction about future copycats: CONTPAQi Bancos, Alegra, misKuentas and Bind ERP already ship overlapping deliverables today, and virtual-CFO despachos already sell your Phase 1 assisted-service model at overlapping prices. You are not being copied — you are entering occupied ground and calling it 7/10.

comparables.name: Alegra Contabilidad
comparables.what: Cloud accounting for LATAM SMBs. Pulls CFDI directly from the SAT and registers it in the books in one click, connects bank accounts or ingests CSV/XML statements, automates reconciliation, and markets cash-flow statements, trial balance, income statement and AR/AP reporting plus IVA, DIOT and RESICO calculation. Builds explicitly for despachos with multi-RFC included at no extra cost per RFC. From roughly MXN 499/month.
comparables.difference: Ships most of your deliverables for one-fifth to one-twentieth of your price and owns your distribution channel. You add human review, forecasting and three recommended actions. That is your entire wedge, and it is a feature Alegra could ship in a sprint — while simultaneously being the price anchor every prospect will quote back at you.

comparables.name: CONTPAQi Bancos
comparables.what: Bank reconciliation module inside Mexico's dominant SMB accounting suite. Reads layouts from the major Mexican banks, matches movements by amount, date and reference, integrates with the SAT's Administrador de Documentos Digitales to validate received CFDI, and shows a reconciliation dashboard with a traffic-light view of matched, pending and discrepant movements. CONTPAQi is now actively marketing AI and automation content.
comparables.difference: Owns the installed base through accountants — which means your gatekeeper already has this on his desk. Your advantage is that CONTPAQi is contador-facing and produces compliance output, not an owner-facing weekly decision brief. Your disadvantage is that changing that is a UI project for them and a company for you.

comparables.name: Xepelin
comparables.what: Mexican SMB finance platform: receivables and payables plus a financial dashboard built off SAT data, alongside working-capital financing.
comparables.difference: The closest thing to your core in the fintech layer, and it monetises through credit — meaning it can give a cash forecast away free forever. Treat this as prior art until you have personally verified what it ships. If Xepelin already offers 30/60/90 forecasting to this segment, your only whitespace is gone and the flip to executed collections becomes mandatory rather than advisable.

comparables.name: Clara
comparables.what: Corporate virtual and physical cards plus a spend-control platform with accounting integration; described as LATAM's fastest-growing fintech in the corporate segment.
comparables.difference: Already holds the transaction data and the finance-side relationship, and earns on interchange rather than subscriptions. A cash-position view is a natural bolt-on it can price at zero. Weaker on receivables and on the owner-operator segment below 25 employees — that gap is your window, and windows close.

comparables.name: Belvo ("Fiscal Mexico")
comparables.what: Financial data aggregation across 60+ institutions in Mexico, Brazil and Colombia, plus an explicit SAT/fiscal data product. Alternatives include Finerio Connect and Prometeo.
comparables.difference: Your supplier, not your competitor — which is the finding. The bank-plus-SAT ingestion you listed as defensible integration work is a purchase order any competitor can sign. Also your concentration risk: coverage is thinner than the headline number (one public tracker lists 18 reachable institutions, varying by product), so verify your actual prospects' banks before promising live connections.

comparables.name: Bind ERP
comparables.what: Mexican cloud ERP for SMBs, including a collections module that tracks receivables and automates payment reminders, positioned explicitly around improving cash flow.
comparables.difference: Validates demand for the collections wedge while stopping short of it — Bind sends automated reminders; nobody at Bind phones your client's customer on Tuesday. That distinction between automated nudges and executed human follow-up is the most defensible territory available to you in this market.

comparables.name: Virtual-CFO / fractional finance despachos
comparables.what: Accounting firms upselling "asesoría financiera": human-reviewed cash reporting, forecasting and advisory for SMB owners, typically MXN 8,000–25,000/month, sometimes lower for light packages.
comparables.difference: Your true head-to-head competitor and the reason Phase 1 is not a moat — they already sell a trained human reviewing the numbers and reporting to the owner, with an existing client list and near-zero CAC. Your only edges are cost per client (AI-assisted operators) and consistency of the weekly cadence. Neither is visible to the buyer in a first meeting, which is a positioning problem, not a product problem.
